reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: One of the few treatable congenital disorders of glycosylation, caused by biallelic MPI variants
Distinctive in that intellect and neurological development are usually spared, contrasting with PMM2-CDG
Dominant features are hepatic-intestinal: protein-losing enteropathy, hepatic fibrosis, chronic diarrhoea and failure to thrive
Coagulation disturbance produces both bleeding and thrombotic risk, with low antithrombin, protein C and protein S
Hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia can occur and may be a presenting problem
Serum transferrin analysis shows a type 1 (whole-glycan loss) pattern, indistinguishable from PMM2-CDG on screening
Confirmation is by mannose phosphate isomerase enzyme assay and MPI gene sequencing
Oral mannose supplementation bypasses the enzymatic block and can markedly improve the enteropathy and coagulopathy
reference.pathophysiology: MPI-CDG is caused by deficiency of phosphomannose isomerase, which interconverts fructose-6-phosphate and mannose-6-phosphate. Because mannose-6-phosphate is the precursor for GDP-mannose and the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide used in N-glycosylation, enzyme deficiency limits mannose supply and impairs assembly of the lipid-linked glycan precursor, producing hypoglycosylation of serum and membrane glycoproteins similar to PMM2-CDG. The block lies upstream of the point where free mannose enters the pathway, so providing exogenous mannose (phosphorylated directly to mannose-6-phosphate by hexokinase) restores substrate and largely corrects glycosylation, explaining the disorder's responsiveness to dietary mannose. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and the phenotype centres on the gut, liver and coagulation rather than the brain.
additionalDifferentials: PMM2-CDG and other type 1 CDGs (identical transferrin screening pattern)
Congenital enteropathies and protein-losing enteropathy of other cause
Congenital hepatic fibrosis or neonatal cholestatic liver disease
Inherited thrombophilias and coagulation factor deficiencies
Coeliac disease and other malabsorptive states
additionalInvestigations: Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing/mass spectrometry (type 1 pattern)
Coagulation panel with antithrombin, protein C, protein S
Serum albumin and stool alpha-1-antitrypsin for protein-losing enteropathy
Liver ultrasound/elastography and transaminases for fibrosis
Fasting glucose and insulin studies for hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia
redFlags: Life-threatening gastrointestinal or surgical bleeding from coagulopathy
Venous thrombosis, including portal or cerebral sinus thrombosis
Severe hypoalbuminaemia with oedema from protein-losing enteropathy
Recurrent hypoglycaemia causing seizures or neurological injury
Progressive hepatic fibrosis leading to portal hypertension
reference.prognosis: With early recognition and dietary mannose supplementation the gastrointestinal and coagulation abnormalities often improve substantially and neurodevelopment is typically preserved, although hepatic fibrosis may progress and thrombotic risk persists.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish MPI-CDG from other type 1 CDGs, thereby missing a treatable disorder
Not trialling mannose supplementation because the transferrin screen looks like PMM2-CDG
Overlooking combined bleeding and thrombotic risk when planning procedures
Attributing chronic diarrhoea and hypoalbuminaemia to a primary gut disease alone
Missing hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia as a treatable complication
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
Jaeken J, Inborn Errors of Metabolism: Diagnosis and Treatment
management: Oral D-mannose supplementation is the specific, disease-modifying therapy, bypassing the enzyme block to restore glycosylation and correct the gastrointestinal and coagulation abnormalities
Support the protein-losing enteropathy with nutritional optimisation and albumin replacement, and treat chronic diarrhoea and failure to thrive
Correct the coagulopathy by replacing antithrombin and managing both bleeding and thrombotic complications, anticoagulating for thrombosis
Treat hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia, for example with diazoxide, and maintain glucose supply
Monitor hepatic fibrosis with liver imaging and elastography and manage portal complications
Give thromboprophylaxis around surgery and periods of immobility given the persistent thrombotic risk
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder and test at-risk relatives
Coordinate multidisciplinary metabolic, gastroenterology and haematology care
